lines.trans: I have been living in Moscow for two weeks already.
Have you already gotten used to life in Moscow?
I came here from Voronezh for a dream.
And now you work in the best restaurant.
Claude Monet restaurant is the most famous in the city.
Here there are very strict rules and an expensive menu.
But for me this is wonderful experience.
And where did you find yourself housing?
I live right in the center of the city.
Apartments in the center cost huge money.
And I do not pay a single kopeck!
That sounds very strange and suspicious.
I have one secret plan.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'where'.

examples.text: А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
examples.trans: Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'town, city' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: 'два' with masculine/neuter nouns, 'две' with feminine; the noun goes into the genitive singular

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: plural only: there is no singular in everyday use

examples.trans: The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: to a loved one, and at the start of letters
to a loved one, and at the start of letters

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.
Declinable neuter noun meaning 'housing', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: We are looking for inexpensive housing.
They are looking for inexpensive housing.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to live'.

examples.trans: I live in a communal flat.

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to sound', forming an aspectual pair with 'прозвучать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to ring') (to be heard) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Вот теперь звучит как настоящий мэр!
examples.trans: Now that sounds like a real mayor!

examples.text: Это звучит очень странно и подозрительно.
examples.trans: That sounds very strange and suspicious.

examples.text: Разве это не звучит великолепно для гостей?
examples.trans: Does that not sound magnificent for the guests?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: + genitive: 'из мэрии' = from the town hall

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'вестный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('famous, well-known').

examples.text: Он самый известный человек в городе.
examples.trans: He is the most famous man in town.

examples.text: Вы сами подумайте. Он самый известный человек в Синеозерске!
examples.trans: Think about it yourselves. He is the most famous man in Sineozersk!

examples.text: Он самый известный человек в Синеозерске!
examples.trans: He is the most famous man in Sineozersk!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'flat', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?

meanings.en: kopeck, one hundredth of a rouble
meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'kopeck' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('not a penny') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: лучший в мире = the best in the world
Secondary conversational sense ('better') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты мне даёшь пятьсот рублей, а я выхожу и покупаю тебе лучшую приставку в мире.
examples.trans: You give me five hundred roubles, and I get out and buy you the best console in the world.

meanings.note: on a phone or in a restaurant; indeclinable

examples.text: Что за меню здесь? Как позвонить?
examples.trans: What's this menu here? How do I make a call?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'dream', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, тебе сколько лет? Это глупые детские мечты.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, how old are you? Those are silly childish dreams.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to find', paired with 'находить'.

examples.text: Ну где я сейчас найду грузчиков?
examples.trans: Well, where am I going to find movers right now?

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
неделю = for a week; через неделю = in a week

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: + genitive: ни копейки = not a penny
Secondary conversational sense ('...  = neither... nor') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('huge, enormous').

examples.text: Кстати, если хочешь, иди к нам в команду. Шансы у нас огромные.
examples.trans: By the way, if you want, join our team. Our chances are huge.

meanings.note: agrees in gender and case with the noun
Secondary conversational sense ('alone') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'experience', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: You will need my rich experience.
This life experience is very valuable.

examples.text: А вот тут вам понадобится мой опыт.
examples.trans: And right here you will need my experience.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'plan' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The mayor came up with a new plan.

examples.text: Но мэр придумал новый план. Сосед мэра теперь пойдёт в мэры.
examples.trans: But the mayor came up with a new plan. The mayor's neighbour will now run for mayor.

meanings.note: платить за + accusative = to pay for

examples.text: А вашу работу вернуть можно. И мы хорошо платим.
examples.trans: But we can get your job back for you. And we pay well.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'suspiciously'.

examples.trans: The cook was behaving very suspiciously.
Why are you so suspiciously clean?

examples.text: Это звучит очень странно и подозрительно.
examples.trans: That sounds very strange and suspicious.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'rule', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (by the rules) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Всё по правилам, как рыцарский турнир.
examples.trans: All by the rules, like a knights' tournament.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('beautiful, wonderful').

examples.text: Посмотри, какой у нас город прекрасный. Озёра, луга.
examples.trans: Look what a beautiful town we have. Lakes, meadows.

meanings.en: to get used to, become accustomed
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'выкнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to get used to'.

examples.text: Я ещё не привык к Москве.
examples.trans: I am not used to Moscow yet.

examples.text: Ты уже привык к жизни в Москве?
examples.trans: Have you already gotten used to life in Moscow?
I got used to working by the law.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to arrive (by vehicle)', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.trans: Which car did you come in?

examples.text: Вика, ты на какой машине сегодня приехала?
examples.trans: Vika, which car did you come in today?

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: forms the superlative: самый главный = the most important
Secondary conversational sense ('the very') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The most important thing is the people.
Do you know the main thing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'екретный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('secret').

examples.text: А почему он на секретном совещании?
examples.trans: And why is he at a secret meeting?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тоить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to cost'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to be worth') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And how much does the console cost?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strange'.

examples.text: Как странно, я ничего об этом не слышал.
examples.trans: How strange, I've heard nothing about it.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трогий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strict, stern').

examples.trans: How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

examples.text: У нас в школе очень строгий директор.
examples.trans: We have a very strict principal at our school.

examples.text: Ой, спина не разгибается! Какая вы строгая, Клавдия Викторовна.
examples.trans: Ow, my back won't straighten! How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: of a town; торговый центр = shopping centre

examples.trans: They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
